newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In - Quickening the pulse of the Internet.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In - Quickening the pulse of the Internet.

text.p: Speed is good. In fact, on the Internet, speed is everything.
So far the Internet has been well suited for the eternally patient. Calling up those pages dripping with complex graphics frustrates all but the most hardy users.
Newcomers to the World Wide Web are often titillated dropping into some of the hotter Web sites and are then quickly underwhelmed by the slowness of it all.
After all, this is the remote control generation that can watch several programs on television at once and find them all boring.
The Web is certainly a step up from the static world of TV, but the problem is molasses-like access times. That probably restrains growth, remarkable as the medium's progress has been.

A recent Nielsen survey found that about one-fifth of North American adults are online, a sizable and growing number, although still a venue dominated by males. There are large blocks of the population not yet enamored with the new medium.

Speedier access times are therefore a must, but it appears industry is aware of the problem. A number of groups have been coming up with a range of solutions, including cable communication modems and the testing of new higher speed phone lines.

This week, Ameritech Corp became the latest Baby Bell to announce, along with IBM Corp, a trial of a high-speed Internet connection known as ADSL, or Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line. Two hundred lucky Chicago-area Internet users will get to turbo-charge their Internet for the next six months.
Ameritech and IBM said this will give the users access 50 times faster than the average phone line and 10 times faster than an ISDN line, the current off-the-shelf speedy communications line.
With ADSL, users will be able to make phone calls while accessing the Web at speeds to be clocked at 1.5 megabits per second.
Ameritech did not disclose what it thinks the line or the modem will cost when the commercial service is rolled out next year.
"We are not speculating prices will be," said Rick Aspan of Ameritech. "That's why we are doing this trial: we want to know if it meets their (the user) needs."

But Ameritech clearly sees strong business demand for the service. "It is ideal for multimedia and data communications, such as remote access to corporate LANs, Internet and desktop videoconferencing..." it said in a news release.
Here is the most important bit: "...it reduces to seconds the amount of time necessary to download complex graphics and information that used to take several minutes."
In other words, in a click of the mouse the home page you have been seeking arrives at your desktop. Just what we have been waiting (too long) for.
Both corporate and personal users will gravitate to the speedier Net access as fast as it becomes available and as soon they can afford it.
But there are a few nagging questions: If we build faster on-ramps with these speedier access lines, will the Net itself become faster?
Won't the main communications backbone that carries all this traffic need to be upgraded just as fast? Will the network servers providing the content on the Net also be expanded sufficiently?
Greg Gapinski, marketing manager for broadband at IBM, believes industry will be able to build the super Internet in time, with a bigger and more robust communications systems.
He said in the near term one solution will be to find out what users in any particular area use most and then have that site "hosted" in the region.
"One serious alternative is to try and take the pulse of the Internet closer to them," he said.
Perhaps a healthier Internet pulse is what we have all been seeking.
(To comment on this weekly column, Russell Blinch can be reached at: russell.blinch@reuters.com)
